title: Control plane ownership handoff canvas notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working workshop doc to map service boundaries and ownership for the control plane pieces that touch routing: API gateway, orchestration layer (regional director, placement, policy engine), and runtime adapters (kube/gpu adapters, private deployment adapters). Goal is a pragmatic handoff canvas so teams can implement clear SLA boundaries and on-call responsibilities for multi-region routing and failover.

Context and constraints (short):
- Traffic must be routable by policy (latency-first, cost-preference, data-sovereignty) with automated failover between regions and model variants.
- Runtime adapters are heterogeneous (hosted GPU pools, dedicated reserved clusters, customer VPCs).
- Observability must provide per-route token-latency and cost breakdowns; token-level tracing is expensive so sample and correlate via request-id.
- Changes need low-friction ownership paths for emergency fallback and rollouts.

High-level components (as we use them in infra):
- API Gateway: ingress, rate limiting, auth, initial validation. Terminates customer TLS and enforces tenant quotas.
- Routing Policy Engine (part of orchestration): evaluates routing rules, region preferences, model variant fallbacks, and returns a candidate runtime set.
- Placement Orchestrator: decides exact runtime instance(s) to use, coordinates slot allocation, and triggers adapter handoff.
- Runtime Adapters: adapters translate orchestrator placement to platform-specific calls (k8s/GPU pools, dedicated host RPCs, private connectors).
- Health & Fallback Controller: keeps per-runtime health and triggers automatic fallback to warm variants/regions.

Ownership proposals (rough matrix in prose):
- API Gateway: eng-platform-engineering / api-gateway subteam. Responsibilities: auth/quota enforcement, ingress throttles, request shaping, API versioning. SLA: 99.95 ingress availability.
- Routing Policy Engine: eng-platform-engineering / policy-team. Responsibilities: rule language, evaluation accuracy, policy rollout framework (canary evaluation). SLA: 99.9 correctness under typical load; degrade to safe default policy on errors.
- Placement Orchestrator: eng-platform-engineering / orchestrator-team. Responsibilities: slot allocation, regional placement heuristics, capacity negotiation with Dedicated. SLA: 99.9 placement success within target latency.
- Runtime Adapters: split ownership depending on adapter type: hosted-adapter (serving-runtime team), dedicated-adapter (platform-engineering + commercial/dedicated infra), private-adapter (private-deployments team). Responsibilities: API surface for start/stop/deploy, health signals, scaling hooks. SLA: adapter-specific (define per-adapter runbook).
- Health & Fallback Controller: SRE + orchestrator-team shared. Responsibilities: define health criteria, circuit-break policies, automated failover windows, and rollback triggers.

Example ownership boundary clarifications (issues we've hit in past):
- If an adapter returns a 500 for placement: adapter team owns root cause; orchestrator must have a fast fallback to compatible adapter.
- If policy engine returns malformed routing decisions: policy-team owns regression; API Gateway must have a defensive validation layer that returns 5xx to caller only after safe defaulting attempts.
- If runtime allocation fails due to capacity (no slots): placement orchestrator owns quota negotiation and triggering burst fallback; capacity forecasting should alert capacity-ops.

Operational interfaces (what each team must expose):
- Health endpoints: standardized probe with fields: component, region, last_success, error_rate_1m, token_latency_p50/95/99 (sampled).
- Control APIs: start/stop/decommission, drain, warm-cache, scale-to. Must be authenticated and idempotent.
- Observability hooks: emit request_id, routing_decision_id, model_variant_id, adapter_id on traces.
- Runbooks: each component must ship a one-page on-call runbook that lists fast mitigation steps and rollback commands.

Routing policy primitives (draft DSL example):
- priority: [latency, cost, sovereignty]
- constraints: { region: [us-west-2, eu-west-1], model_capabilities: [chat, embeddings], max_cost_per_token: 0.0005 }
- fallbacks: [variant-quantized, region-eu, region-us]
Example (pseudo-yaml):
policy: fast-chat-machine
  priority: [latency, cost]
  constraints:
    region: [primary, fallback]
    model: [redwood-3b, redwood-3b-8bit]
  fallbacks:
    - model: redwood-3b-8bit
    - region: eu-west-1

Operational flow (happy path):
1) API Gateway authenticates + rate-limits and enriches with tenant metadata + request_id.
2) Policy Engine evaluates rules, returns ordered candidate list.
3) Placement Orchestrator queries runtime inventory and selects adapter.
4) Adapter allocates slot and returns the endpoint + kv-cache token.
5) Gateway forwards or proxies the session to runtime and observes successful start.
6) Ongoing health checks and token-level sampling feed back to metrics/alerts.

Failure/fallback flow (important):
- If adapter cannot allocate within timeout T_alloc -> orchestrator triggers next candidate immediately.
- If placement takes more than T_slo (configured per tier) -> return in-flight error with safe fallback (queued low-priority or degraded mode), and fire an incident metric.
- If region-wide capacity drop -> orchestrator enacts regional-failover plan and notifies capacity-ops and CS for impacted tenants.

Open questions we need to resolve in next workshop:
- Policy language: how expressive vs how fast? Do we support scriptable matchers or stick to declarative primitives?
- How to represent cost in routing without leaking billing details into control plane decisions (privacy/price fluctuation concerns)?
- Ownership for cross-cutting rollout features (canary policy, staged rollout across regions): policy-team or orchestrator-team?
- SLA contract boundaries: what is the guaranteed latency for checkout (end-to-end) vs component internal SLOs?

Immediate action items (owners listed):
- Draft a 1-page adapter runbook template (owner: Diego Morales) — due 2025-01-20.
- Define health probe schema and proto (owner: Evelyn Park + SRE) — due 2025-01-28.
- Policy DSL proposal: quick prototype showing latency-first and sovereignty-first expressions (owner: Ravi Singh) — due 2025-02-04.
- Incident playbook for region failover (owner: Priya Kapoor + SRE) — due 2025-02-10.

Notes to self / rough ideas (brainstorm fragments):
- Could encode cost as tier-ids (cheap/standard/premium) instead of raw $/token to avoid exposing price movements.
- Consider a lightweight prebaked fallback registry of warm endpoints that orchestrator can hit with single RPC (avoids full adapter allocation latency).
- For private adapters, require a heartbeat token from the customer's VPC connector before offering them as primary. If heartbeat stale -> mark as warm-only.

Decision log (working):
- 2025-01-15: Agreed to require per-adapter runbooks and standardized health probes. (tentative)
- 2025-01-20: Decided to prototype policy DSL as declarative first, with hooks for extension.

Attachments / references (links inline above):
- Confluence reference page for the canvas and prior ownership sketches.
- Jira epic for work: PLT-423.
- Draft PR for orchestration APIs on github.

This doc is intentionally informal — capture handwritten notes from the Jan workshop and action items. We'll convert the final ownership table into a single CSV and a follow-up Confluence page once the draft runbooks and health probes are merged.

End of notes.
